common_name: Barton Pecan (Early USDA Texas Pecan, Prone to Alternate Bearing)

planting.note: Plant a grafted bare-root tree in late winter to early spring once the ground can be worked, in a deep, well-drained site with a same-season pollen-compatible pecan nearby; expect heavy on-years to need mid-summer hand or shaker thinning to reduce alternate bearing.

directions: Barton was the first pecan released by the USDA pecan breeding program, bred from a 1937 Moore x Success cross made in the orchard of John Barton Sr. near Utley, Texas, under USDA breeder L.D. Romberg's program, and released in 1953. It bears a large, good-quality nut (about 48 to the pound, 57% kernel) with scab resistance that has held up well over decades, but the tree is infamous for severe alternate bearing that leaves it overloaded with poorly filled nuts the year after a heavy crop. Gulf Coast growers can even out production by shaking or hand-thinning the developing crop in on-years, which keeps nut fill and tree vigor more consistent. Its disease tolerance makes it a reasonable pick for humid Southern gardens willing to manage its boom-and-bust habit.
sources: USDA-ARS National Clonal Germplasm Repository for Pecan

common_name: Chickasaw Pecan (Early Mid-Season Texas USDA Pecan)

planting.note: Set grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil; because Chickasaw sheds pollen in midseason but is pistillate-receptive early, pair it with a Type I pollenizer cultivar for reliable nut set.

directions: Chickasaw was bred by USDA-ARS pecan breeder L.D. Romberg at Brownwood, Texas from a 1944 Brooks x Evers cross and released in 1972. It is a protogynous (Type II) cultivar, precocious and heavy-bearing, that ripens roughly two and a half weeks ahead of the old-line Stuart variety. Like many early Texas releases it tends toward alternate bearing once the tree matures, so periodic crop thinning helps keep nut quality even from year to year. Note that its scab resistance is strongest in its native Texas; growers in more humid areas like south Louisiana or Georgia should expect more disease pressure. Its earlier harvest window can be a real advantage for Gulf Coast growers racing to beat fall rains or squirrel pressure.
sources: USDA-ARS National Clonal Germplasm Repository for Pecan (Texas A&M pecan database)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in early spring in a sunny, well-drained site; as a mid-October-harvest selection it benefits from the long, warm growing season typical of Gulf Coast gardens.

directions: Carter is a large-nutted pecan cultivar associated with Alabama growers, typically reaching harvest around mid-October, which places it in the midseason group for Deep South orchards. Some years produce visible kernel veining, a cosmetic trait noted in University of Georgia extension records on the variety. Published detail on its exact origin and parentage is thin, so it is best treated as a regionally known but lightly documented selection worth confirming with a local extension office before planting at scale. For home growers it offers another large-nut, heat-adapted option alongside the area's better-documented named cultivars.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension (Pecan Trees for the Home or Backyard Orchard, B1348)

common_name: Dooley Pecan (Historic Scab-Susceptible Oklahoma Native Pecan)

planting.note: Because this cultivar is scab-susceptible, Gulf Coast growers should choose a drier, well-ventilated inland site or plan a fungicide program rather than siting it in the most humid coastal locations.

directions: Dooley is a native pecan selection found near Okmulgee, Oklahoma, and was once a widely favored variety in Oklahoma orchards before more disease-resistant releases became common. It produces a moderate-sized nut averaging around 46 percent kernel and ripens about 17 days after Pawnee on a protandrous (Type I) flowering schedule, sheding pollen before its own female flowers are receptive. Because Dooley is scab-susceptible, it performs best on drier inland Southern sites or under a regular fungicide program rather than in the most humid stretches of the Gulf Coast. Today it is of most interest as a historic regional selection grown by collectors of older Oklahoma and Kansas pecan varieties.
sources: Northern Pecans (William Reid, Kansas State University Pecan Experiment Field)
USDA-ARS National Clonal Germplasm Repository for Pecan

common_name: Farley Pecan (Thin-Shelled Florida Panhandle Heirloom Pecan)

planting.note: Plant in full sun on deep, well-drained soil in early spring; because the thin shell is very attractive to squirrels and other wildlife, consider netting or exclusion around harvest time if growing for your own crop.

directions: Farley was discovered around 1918 growing in Jackson County in the Florida panhandle and was introduced commercially about 1925 by B.W. Stone's Stone Nursery Company of Thomasville, Georgia. It is prized for an unusually thin shell (around 62 nuts per pound, 51% kernel) and sweet, well-flavored kernels, though its parentage was never recorded. Farley ripens late in the season, and because squirrels and other wildlife find the thin shell just as easy to open as people do, home growers may need to protect a developing crop. Its Deep South origin gives it naturally good heat and humidity tolerance for coastal Gulf gardens.
sources: University of Georgia Pecan Breeding Program (pecanbreeding.uga.edu)
USDA-ARS National Clonal Germplasm Repository for Pecan

common_name: Giles Pecan (Kansas Native Pecan, Crooked-Nut Heirloom Selection)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in early spring; this cold-hardy, vigorous native selection tolerates Southern humidity but is grown more for reliability and as breeding stock than for uniform nut appearance.

directions: Giles is a native pecan tree discovered in the Neosho River floodplain near Chetopa, Kansas, in A.E. Giles's grove, and named in 1930; it went on to become the dominant orchard cultivar in Kansas through the 1970s. Its nuts are easy to recognize in the field by their characteristic crooked, asymmetrical shape, and the tree is valued chiefly for reliable production and cold hardiness (it is protandrous, around 52% kernel, but scab-susceptible and a strong alternate bearer) rather than nut uniformity. Jayhawk, a direct seedling selection of Giles, has gone on to prove useful further south across the Southern pecan belt, and Giles itself can still serve Southern yards as a hardy, low-input shade-and-nut tree. Today it functions mainly as a genetic resource and historic parent line rather than a top choice for a humid coastal orchard.
sources: Northern Pecans (William Reid, Kansas State University Pecan Experiment Field)
USDA-ARS National Clonal Germplasm Repository for Pecan

common_name: Jayhawk Pecan (Scab-Resistant Kansas Pecan with Mottled Kernel)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in early spring in full sun; its scab resistance and precocity suit a disease-tolerant home orchard where occasional cosmetic kernel mottling is an acceptable tradeoff for reliable cropping.

directions: Jayhawk is a seedling of Giles originated by Lewis Harris of Wichita, Kansas, and named in 1989. It is precocious and productive with good scab resistance and a medium-thin shell (about 51% kernel), though its kernels sometimes show darker mottled or blotchy patches that make the nut meat less visually appealing despite acceptable flavor, and it ripens about ten days after the Pawnee standard. Gulf Coast growers wanting a disease-tolerant pecan for a home orchard may find Jayhawk useful where reliable cropping matters more than cosmetic kernel appearance. As with other Kansas-origin pecans, it brings strong vigor and cold tolerance into a Southern planting.
sources: Northern Pecans (William Reid, Kansas State University Pecan Experiment Field)
Kansas State University Research and Extension

common_name: Maramec Pecan (Late-Season Oklahoma Pecan, Mahan Seedling)

planting.note: Plant in early spring in deep, well-drained soil; expect to manage scab pressure with a fungicide program in humid climates, and plan on summer hand-thinning of the nut crop in heavy on-years to protect kernel quality.

directions: Maramec is a seedling of the Mahan cultivar found in Pawnee County, Oklahoma, and named in 1969. It flowers on a protogynous (Type II) schedule and ripens about 26 days after the Pawnee standard, placing it in the late-season group, but is only moderately scab resistant to susceptible, so Gulf Coast growers in humid areas should expect to manage scab with a fungicide program or accept some crop loss in wet years. The tree develops an attractive, well-structured form but becomes a severe alternate bearer as it matures, so Gulf Coast growers should plan on summer nut thinning in heavy on-years to maintain kernel quality and tree vigor.
sources: Northern Pecans (William Reid, Kansas State University Pecan Experiment Field)

common_name: Waccamaw Pecan (Pecan Named for the Waccamaw People of Coastal South Carolina)

planting.note: Treat as a trial selection: plant one grafted tree alongside a well-documented, proven scab-resistant cultivar so a Gulf Coast garden still has a reliable nut source if Waccamaw underperforms locally.

directions: Waccamaw is a seedling pecan of unknown parentage found near Golden City, Missouri, and named by its discoverer after the Waccamaw people of coastal South Carolina rather than for its place of origin. Its nuts run slightly smaller than Pawnee with a kernel percentage in the mid-50s, flowering is protandrous, and it ripens just a few days after Pawnee. Documentation of this cultivar comes mainly from a single Kansas pecan-breeding source, and accounts of its scab resistance are genuinely mixed even within that source, so Gulf Coast gardeners should treat a planting as somewhat experimental rather than assume the disease tolerance of better-documented Southern releases. It is best suited to growers curious about trialing an unusual, lightly documented regional selection rather than those wanting a proven commercial Southern pecan.
sources: Northern Pecans (William Reid, Kansas State University Pecan Experiment Field)
